value.overview: The Paint-billed Crake is a small, secretive rail of wetlands, wet grasslands, damp thickets, and other areas with dense ground cover. Its strongly reddish bill, olive-brown upperparts, gray face and underparts, and reddish legs are distinctive when it is seen well. The species is difficult to observe because it usually moves quietly through vegetation, but it may emerge into open ground or shallow water to feed, especially around dawn and dusk.
value.classification: The Paint-billed Crake belongs to the rail family Rallidae and the order Gruiformes. Its accepted scientific name is Mustelirallus erythrops; Neocrex erythrops is an older name still encountered in some references.
value.identification: This crake is about 20 to 23 cm long and has a compact, short-tailed shape typical of rails. Adults show olive-brown or brown upperparts, a gray head and breast, a white throat, and reddish or pinkish legs. The bill is relatively stout, arched, and bright red to reddish-orange, often with a darker tip. It is most often detected by brief views as it walks or runs between grasses and wetland vegetation rather than by prolonged observation.
value.rangeHabitat: The species has a broad but patchy distribution from Costa Rica and Panama through northern and western South America, with additional populations in the Amazon Basin, southeastern Brazil, and the Galápagos Islands. In Costa Rica it is a rare or local resident, recorded mainly in suitable lowland and foothill habitats, including wet grassland, freshwater marshes, damp fields, ditches, and dense vegetation near water. It can also occur in human-modified landscapes where moist cover remains available.
value.migrationStatus: Paint-billed Crakes are generally considered resident, and there is no well-established regular long-distance migration pattern. Movements are poorly known; individuals may make local movements in response to water levels and habitat conditions. In Costa Rica, available checklists treat the species as resident, although its secretive behavior and scattered records make seasonal patterns difficult to determine.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited and varies across the species' large range. A documented study confirmed breeding in Costa Rica, showing that the country is part of the species' breeding range rather than only a nonbreeding area. The nest is a cup or bowl of green grass placed on or near the ground and partly concealed in dense vegetation. Reported clutches contain about three to seven creamy-buff eggs marked with reddish blotches; incubation lasts at least about 23 to 25 days.
value.dietFeeding: The diet is not well documented, but known foods include invertebrates such as beetles and millipedes, along with seeds. The crake forages on soil, leaf litter, and in shallow or standing water, probing and picking food from wet ground and vegetation. It may leave dense cover to feed in more open areas during the cooler, dimmer periods around dawn and dusk, when it is less exposed to predators.
value.behavior: The Paint-billed Crake is furtive and usually solitary or encountered in pairs. It walks and runs through grass, marsh vegetation, and leaf litter, often freezing or slipping back into cover when disturbed. Its voice includes a gradually accelerating series of short, yelping notes, as well as guttural, buzzy, purring, and sharp calls. Because it is hard to see and rarely remains in the open, vocal surveys and careful searching of suitable cover are useful for detecting it.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is unknown. The species is difficult to survey, and reliable population estimates are not available.
